item.title: Economic Watch: Cross-Strait semiconductor firms eye cooperation, new opportunities
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-07
Economic Watch: Cross-Strait semiconductor firms eye cooperation, new opportunities TAIPEI, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Chinese mainland and Taiwan semiconductor companies taking part in SEMICON Taiwan 2026 -- a world-leading specialized semiconductor exhibition -- expressed their willingness to pool complementary strengths and embrace new opportunities. The three-day exhibition concluded on Friday at the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center. Organized by the global semiconductor industry association SEMI, the annual event was first held in September 1996, covering the entire semiconductor supply chain, including equipment, materials, packaging and testing. This year it brought together more than 1,300 exhibitors and hosted over 4,300 booths. A number of mainland companies attended the exhibition and presented their latest products, offering a glimpse of the potential to share new opportunities in the rapidly evolving semiconductor industry on both sides of the Taiwan Strait. At the booth of Huangshan Juxin New Material Co., Ltd., samples of materials in various sizes and colors were neatly displayed, drawing inquiries from Taiwan industry professionals. "Many Taiwan companies have shown strong interest in our products, and some visitors are friends we met at last year's exhibition," said Qu Chao, the company's sales director. The high-tech company, which specializes in high-performance polyimide materials, was attending the exhibition for the second time. "Polyimide materials are used throughout the semiconductor industry, from front-end chip manufacturing to back-end packaging," Qu said, adding that Juxin's products offer competitive prices, customized services and full traceability. "There is considerable room for greater cross-Strait industrial cooperation," Qu said, adding that with Taiwan possessing a well-developed semiconductor supply chain, materials from mainland suppliers could be further processed by local companies and applied across a wider range of fields. At the booth of Taiwan-based Veego Corporation, anti-reflective optical windows and gold-coated quartz panels were displayed under bright lights. The products were manufactured by Lianyungang Huide Quartz Glass Co., Ltd., and were being exhibited in Taiwan for the first time through Veego Corporation. "We are optimistic about the quality and potential of mainland quartz products," said Chuang Ya-hui of Veego Corporation, noting that the two companies established their partnership last year, hoping to introduce the products to more Taiwan customers and explore additional applications. Other mainland exhibitors also used the event to explore more advanced forms of industrial cooperation. Anchu Technology Co., Ltd., based in the eastern Chinese city of Zhangjiagang, specializes in formulated functional electronic chemicals and the safe storage of electronic specialty gases for semiconductor manufacturing. The company brought its flagship product -- a negative-pressure gas cylinder designed for the safe storage of high-purity electronic gases -- to this year's exhibition. "We believe the product has strong competitiveness in the Taiwan market," said Jing Shaoqing, the company's marketing director. Anchu Technology has participated in the exhibition for three consecutive years and consistently received enthusiastic inquiries from Taiwan businesses, Jing said. The exhibition came as Taiwan's semiconductor industry faces growing pressure to expand production overseas, particularly in the United States, as industrial insiders warned of a broader U.S. strategy to establish a whole supply chain that increasingly sidelines Taiwan. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC), the world's leading contract chipmaker and a cornerstone of Taiwan's technology industry, has become a central focus of those efforts. The company has announced massive investments in Arizona, while its suppliers in Taiwan are also facing increasing pressure to expand operations in the United States. Against this backdrop, industry observers are calling for diversifying markets and strengthening industrial links. "The two sides of the Strait have strong complementarities in terms of semiconductor applications and markets," said Lo Huai-jia, secretary-general of the Taiwan R&D Managers Association. Noting that the mainland is one of the world's most important manufacturing bases, Lo said as its manufacturing sector continues to develop, demand for semiconductor products and the range of their applications are also expected to expand. "The complementary strengths of industries on both sides of the Strait could create much broader room for cooperation," Lo added.

item.title: Taiwan Affairs Office of Xingyang Organizes Compatriots and Families of Taiwan Origin to Experience Intangible Cultural Heritage
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
Taiwan Affairs Office of Xingyang Organizes Compatriots and Families of Taiwan Origin to Experience Intangible Cultural Heritage Source: Taiwan.cnUpdated: 2026-09-04
Sep 4(Taiwan.cn)—On August 27, the Taiwan Affairs Office of Xingyang organized representatives of Taiwan compatriots and their family members residing locally to take part in an immersive observation？and？experience activity featuring intangible cultural heritage. During the event, participants visited distinctive cultural sites including the Chang？style Boxing Training Institute, the Yellow River Chengni Inkstone Art Museum, and the Hou？dian Village Hollow？out Cultural and Creative Park to learn about the preservation and inheritance of local intangible cultural heritage resources. With on？site briefings, craft demonstrations and interactive hands？on sessions, Taiwan compatriots and their families gained detailed insights into the historical evolution, inheritance lineage, technical features and inheritance system of each intangible cultural heritage item. Rooted in Xingyang’s local intangible cultural heritage resources, the activity allowed Taiwan compatriots and their families to get close？up exposure to the profound heritage and humanistic spirit of traditional martial arts, craftsmanship and folk arts. It further deepened their understanding of the historical bonds that bind people across the Taiwan Strait as one origin with shared culture and ethnicity. (Jointly reported by Taiwan.cn and the Taiwan Affairs Office of Xingyang) Related Stories

item.title: China Coast Guard patrols waters east of Taiwan Island
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-03
China Coast Guard patrols waters east of Taiwan Island Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-09-03
BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- The China Coast Guard (CCG) on Thursday conducted routine law-enforcement patrols in the waters east of China's Taiwan Island in accordance with the law, a spokesperson said. Jiang Lue, a spokesperson for the CCG, said a CCG task group led by the ship Putuoshan has been strengthening control over the relevant waters since August to effectively ensure orderly navigation and activities, safeguarding the legitimate and lawful rights and interests, as well as the lives and property of Chinese people from both sides of the Taiwan Strait. The CCG will continue to strengthen law-enforcement patrols in the waters under China's jurisdiction and resolutely safeguard China's territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests, the spokesperson said. item.title: China completes marine geophysical survey in waters east of its Taiwan Island
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-03
China completes marine geophysical survey in waters east of its Taiwan Island Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-09-03
BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- China conducted a comprehensive marine geophysical survey in waters east of its Taiwan Island from Aug. 10 to 31, the Ministry of Natural Resources said on Thursday. The survey, carried out by the Second Institute of Oceanography under the ministry, was aimed at gaining a comprehensive understanding of the basic geological conditions and seabed structural features of waters under China's jurisdiction, and supporting the development of a digital platform for natural resources administration and territorial-spatial planning. It collected basic data on the seabed environment, including seafloor topography, sedimentary strata, deep geological structures and geophysical fields. The data will help China further understand the seabed geological and geophysical characteristics of this area, and provide data for geological research on seabed sedimentation and tectonic structures, as well as deep crustal structure and geodynamic evolution in waters east of Taiwan Island, according to the ministry. The survey also provides a scientific basis for China's integrated governance of waters under its jurisdiction in the region. Related Stories

item.title: Mainland expresses thanks to various sectors in Taiwan for concern over mudslide disaster
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-02
Mainland expresses thanks to various sectors in Taiwan for concern over mudslide disaster Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-09-02
BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday expressed appreciation to people from various sectors in Taiwan for their concern after a devastating mudslide struck Gyirong border Port in southwest Xizang Autonomous Region. "No one from Taiwan was reported missing, hurt or dead from the disaster," said Zhang Han, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office. "We will keep following the situation and provide necessary assistance in a timely manner to Taiwan compatriots in the stricken area," she said. An ice-rock avalanche in Nepal triggered a deadly mudslide that hit Gyirong Port on the Chinese side on Aug. 26. According to the latest update of the Xizang regional government, the disaster has claimed 16 lives and left 546 others missing at the border port. In response to a media question, Zhang expressed concern over the disruption to normal life and work caused by continuous heavy rain in southern Taiwan and willingness to provide help. item.title: Mainland denounces Taiwan authorities' move to increase defense spending
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-02
Mainland denounces Taiwan authorities' move to increase defense spending Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-09-02
BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday criticized the decision of Taiwan authorities led by Lai Ching-te to raise the island's defense budget in 2027, saying it would only bring grave disaster to the people in Taiwan. Zhang Han, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks in response to a question about the island's defense budget of more than 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars (about 31 billion U.S. dollars) for 2027, which Taiwan authorities led by Lai Ching-te said was aimed at strengthening its defense capabilities and demonstrating its resolve to defend itself. Zhang said Taiwan authorities led by Lai Ching-te have stubbornly adhered to their separatist stance of seeking "Taiwan independence," disregarding the mainstream public opinion on the island that calls for "peace, development, cross-Strait exchanges and cooperation." They have instead stoked confrontation across the Taiwan Strait and squandered public funds in pursuit of their independence agenda, Zhang said, adding that such efforts are "simply beyond their capabilities" and will only have serious consequences for the people of Taiwan. "We are unwavering in our resolve and formidable in our ability to safeguard national sovereignty and territorial integrity, and will never leave any room for separatist activities seeking 'Taiwan independence' in any form," Zhang noted. She called on people in Taiwan to recognize the dangers of "Taiwan independence" separatism, firmly oppose such activities, and safeguard the common home of the Chinese nation. Taiwan's executive authorities approved the island's 2027 general budget on Aug. 20, with defense spending rising sharply to over 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars for the first time. The defense budget accounts for roughly 29 percent of total government expenditure, meaning that about 29 out of every 100 New Taiwan dollars in government spending would go toward defense. item.title: Economic Watch: Structural imbalances persist amid Taiwan's economic growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-31
Economic Watch: Structural imbalances persist amid Taiwan's economic growth Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-08-31
TAIPEI, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Recent economic data from Taiwan show a widening gap between a booming high-tech manufacturing sector and traditional industries that continue to struggle. Industry groups and economists on the island say the persistent imbalances call for a more balanced allocation of industrial resources, so that the rapid expansion of one sector does not come at the expense of others. That concern was highlighted in a 2026 report released last week by the Taiwan Federation of Industries, following a survey of 161 industry associations affiliated with the federation. The report said Taiwan authorities have for years placed disproportionate policy emphasis on semiconductors and other high-tech industries. The policy bias has helped drive the tech sector's strong growth, with exports reaching record highs and wealth generated by the tech boom pushing up asset and housing prices. Meanwhile, workers in traditional manufacturing have faced stagnant wages and rising living costs. The contrast, the report said, has created a veneer of prosperity in the statistics while exposing deeper structural strains in Taiwan's economy. The latest trade and industrial production data show how the structural imbalances are playing out across industries. Export orders for information and communications technology products jumped 89.5 percent in July from a year earlier, while orders for electronic products also posted strong growth, according to figures released by Taiwan's economic authorities. By contrast, several traditional industries saw weak demand in July. Orders for chemicals and plastic and rubber products edged up only slightly year on year, while those for optical products fell by more than 10 percent. The divergence was even more striking in industrial production. In July, Taiwan's output of computers, electronics and optical products surged 95.62 percent from a year earlier. Yet production in several traditional industries, including chemicals, fertilizers and automobiles, declined. Taiwan's labor market also shows a structural mismatch. Taiwan's statistics authorities reported that the unemployment rate among people aged 15 to 24 stood at 11.71 percent in July, well above the overall unemployment rate. At the same time, businesses continue to report difficulty finding workers. Some 76.6 percent of the industry associations surveyed for the 2026 report identified labor shortages as their biggest challenge, making it the top concern for the third consecutive year. The coexistence of relatively high youth unemployment and widespread labor shortages points to a mismatch between the jobs being created and the skills available to fill them, according to Tsai Ming-fang, an economics professor at Tamkang University. As technology-driven sectors demand increasingly specialized skills, some job seekers face higher barriers to entering those industries, Tsai said. The disconnect is particularly striking against the backdrop of Taiwan's strong economic growth. Taiwan's statistics agency reported in late July that the island's gross domestic product expanded 12.92 percent year on year in the second quarter. With AI-related exports and investment continuing to surge, Taiwan is on course for potentially double-digit economic growth this year. Yet promising prospects for economic growth have not translated into a comparable improvement in consumer sentiment. Taiwan's widely followed consumer confidence index stood at 65.01 in August, remaining well below 100, the threshold separating optimism from pessimism. The report also highlighted the deep integration of industrial chains on both sides of the Taiwan Strait and the importance of the mainland market, calling on Taiwan authorities to support healthy and orderly cross-Strait exchanges and help Taiwan businesses better share in the opportunities arising from the mainland's development. item.title: Taiwan's DPP authorities pose biggest barrier to cross-Strait exchanges: spokeswoman
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-27
Taiwan's DPP authorities pose biggest barrier to cross-Strait exchanges: spokeswoman BEIJING -- Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities have been acting as the biggest barrier to cross-Strait exchanges, a mainland spokeswoman said on Wednesday. Zhang Han, spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks at a news conference when asked for comments on the DPP authorities' tight vetting on students applying for education exchange programs on the mainland. "The DPP authorities have gone extreme lengths to obstruct normal education and youth exchanges across the Strait," Zhang said, noting that the move has exposed their malicious agenda of escalating cross-Strait confrontation and antagonism. Peace, development, exchanges and cooperation represent mainstream public opinion in Taiwan, said Zhang. "The desire of compatriots across the Strait for closer ties and the momentum of exchanges and cooperation are unstoppable." While revealing that the DPP authorities are intentionally creating "information cocoon" in Taiwan, Zhang extended an invitation to the people of Taiwan to visit the mainland and see the real mainland for themselves. The spokeswoman also called on people from Taiwan to stay clear-headed in the face of Taiwan leader Lai Ching-te's separatist rhetoric and take a firm stand against "Taiwan independence" separatist acts.

item.title: Comment on Taiwan TV draws criticism on both sides of the Strait
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-27
Comment on Taiwan TV draws criticism on both sides of the Strait A comment made on a Taiwan TV program claiming that "there are no refrigerators in Beijing" has drawn criticism on both sides of the Taiwan Strait. "Such remarks, which are detached from reality, will only make a laughingstock of themselves," Zhang Han, a spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular news conference on Wednesday. She said the Democratic Progressive Party authorities have imposed restrictions on and obstructed cross-Strait exchanges and interactions, deliberately creating an "information cocoon" on the island in an attempt to prevent Taiwan residents from learning about the mainland. "We welcome Taiwan residents to break through these barriers, visit the mainland more often and see for themselves the real and vibrant mainland," Zhang said. On a Taiwan TV program called Newswawawa, Liao Mei-ran, a self-described "fortune teller", claimed that during a visit to the mainland, she found "there were no refrigerators in Beijing, and people in Beijing did not have cold drinks". The remark drew attention on both sides of the Strait. Some Taiwan netizens said it reflected the extent to which the island has become an "information cocoon". "While it may appear that you are mocking the mainland, in fact, it is Taiwan that is embarrassing itself," one commenter wrote.

item.title: Tanghe County Hosts Intangible Cultural Heritage Experience for Taiwan Compatriots and Relatives
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
Tanghe County Hosts Intangible Cultural Heritage Experience for Taiwan Compatriots and Relatives Source: Taiwan.cnUpdated: 2026-08-25
Aug 25(Taiwan.cn)—To promote China’s fine traditional culture, enrich the cultural lives of local Taiwan compatriots and their relatives, deepen cross-Strait cultural integration, and foster shared identity, the Taiwan Affairs Office of Tanghe County, Nanyang City, hosted a hands-on experience event featuring Song-style brocade round fans on August 19. Using intangible cultural heritage as an emotional bond, the event helped further bridge the psychological distance between compatriots across the Strait. At the venue, staff provided a detailed introduction to the cultural significance of Song brocade and the auspicious meanings associated with round fans. With pre-prepared materials-including brocade fabric, fan ribs, and tassels-they demonstrated the entire production process step by step. Participants received hands-on guidance on fabric bonding, accessory assembly, and fan-surface finishing, while their questions during the process were answered in detail. The Taiwan compatriots and their relatives focused intently on their creations and exchanged ideas with one another. By carefully cutting fabric, applying adhesives, and decorating with tassels, each participant completed their own unique intangible-heritage round fan. Through this immersive experience, attendees gained a firsthand appreciation for the charm of traditional intangible cultural crafts and developed a deeper understanding of the shared cultural roots that unite compatriots across the Strait.(Jointly reported by Taiwan.cn and the Taiwan Affairs Office of Tanghe County, Nanyang City) Related Stories
